virals.name: AJ Signal
virals.hook:
Iran has named its price for ending the war, and how the demand is built tells us a lot more than the demands themselves...

Tehran is working two lists at the same time. The short one, the version @araghchi takes to the @UN and the OIC, asks for three things to reopen Hormuz. 

Lift the naval blockade, lift the oil sanctions, end the war on every front for good.

The long one, the version the military repeats after each US strike, runs to seven, adding the frozen funds, war compensation, a US pullback from the region, and guarantees against the next attack.

Nearly ALL of those seven go back to the Islamabad Memorandum (the MOU), the deal signed on 17 June that fell apart in July after CENTCOM struck in the middle of it. 

That is why Tehran calls them demands and not requests. It frames the whole list as enforcement, a call for Trump and America to carry out what it says was already agreed, which lets a long and maximal set of asks pass as keeping an old promise.

And the standoff narrows to one question. Iran will touch the nuclear file ONLY once its seven are met. 

Trump wants the nuclear file handled first. Each is telling the other to go first, and neither will, because the one who moves first gives away his leverage to a side that already watched a deal between them fall apart halfway.

What divides them is a trust problem, NOT an argument over terms. Each needs the other to give something up first, and with no referee to guarantee the order, neither can afford to move. 

A war that neither side can afford to end is a war that keeps running.

The three-item list is most likely the real floor. The other four are chips, and the ground Washington will yield last, compensation and pulling its troops back, is the ground any deal will show first.

outsiders.name: AJ Signal
outsiders.hook:
Iran has named its price for ending the war, and how the demand is built tells us a lot more than the demands themselves...

Tehran is working two lists at the same time. The short one, the version @araghchi takes to the @UN and the OIC, asks for three things to reopen Hormuz. 

Lift the naval blockade, lift the oil sanctions, end the war on every front for good.

The long one, the version the military repeats after each US strike, runs to seven, adding the frozen funds, war compensation, a US pullback from the region, and guarantees against the next attack.

Nearly ALL of those seven go back to the Islamabad Memorandum (the MOU), the deal signed on 17 June that fell apart in July after CENTCOM struck in the middle of it. 

That is why Tehran calls them demands and not requests. It frames the whole list as enforcement, a call for Trump and America to carry out what it says was already agreed, which lets a long and maximal set of asks pass as keeping an old promise.

And the standoff narrows to one question. Iran will touch the nuclear file ONLY once its seven are met. 

Trump wants the nuclear file handled first. Each is telling the other to go first, and neither will, because the one who moves first gives away his leverage to a side that already watched a deal between them fall apart halfway.

What divides them is a trust problem, NOT an argument over terms. Each needs the other to give something up first, and with no referee to guarantee the order, neither can afford to move. 

A war that neither side can afford to end is a war that keeps running.

The three-item list is most likely the real floor. The other four are chips, and the ground Washington will yield last, compensation and pulling its troops back, is the ground any deal will show first.

ideas.title: Two returns, two answers
ideas.visual: Split card: left, 1979 plane photo of Khomeini with his one-word answer; right, a recent portrait of the Crown Prince with his answer about kissing the soil. Lion-and-Sun corner mark, sources in the caption.
ideas.angle: Contrast Khomeini's reported 'nothing' on returning to Iran with the Crown Prince's answer on the Schreiber podcast that he would first kiss the soil he left 47 years ago.
